# Greetings

Saying hello in German depends on the time of day and on how well the two people know each other.

A German greeting is a small choice between formal and casual, and most of the choice comes from the clock. Shops, offices and strangers get the time of day. Friends and family get something shorter. The same split runs through goodbyes, so a handful of phrases covers almost every meeting.

## When to use it

- Walking into a shop or an office.
- Meeting a friend on the street.
- Leaving a party.

## Key phrases

### Saying hello

| Phrase | Notes |
|---|---|
| {stack}`Guten Morgen \| Good morning` | Used until about noon. |
| {stack}`Hallo \| Hello` | With friends and family. |

### Saying goodbye

| Phrase | Notes |
|---|---|
| {stack}`Auf Wiedersehen \| Goodbye` | Formal. |
| {stack}`Tschüss \| Bye` | Casual. |

## Formal or casual

Strangers and customers get the formal greeting. Friends and family get the short one.

:::{div} ol-examples
Guten Tag, Frau Weber.
: Good day, Ms Weber.

Hallo, Anna.
: Hello, Anna.
:::

## Culture note

Regional greetings such as *Moin* in the north say more about a place than about the time of day.

## Hear it in practice

:::{audio-examples}
:track: a1/concepts/greetings
:title: Begrüßungen
:title-en: Greetings

Guten Morgen, Frau Weber.
: Good morning, Ms Weber.

Guten Tag, Herr Schmidt.
: Good day, Mr Schmidt.

Guten Abend, Maria.
: Good evening, Maria.

Hallo, Anna.
: Hello, Anna.

Hallo, Max.
: Hello, Max.

Wie geht es Ihnen?
: How are you?

Wie geht's?
: How is it going?

Auf Wiedersehen, Frau Weber.
: Goodbye, Ms Weber.

Tschüss, Anna.
: Bye, Anna.

Bis morgen.
: See you tomorrow.

Bis später.
: See you later.

Gute Nacht.
: Good night.
:::

## Summary

:::{admonition} Key points
:class: note

- The time of day decides the formal greeting.
- Friends and family get the short one.
:::
